title: The storm and the tombs (Luke 8:22–39)
hookLine: he stills a storm, then heals a man living among graves
tomorrow: your faith has made you well

lines: LET US GO OVER TO THE OTHER SIDE.
A STORM CAME DOWN ON THE LAKE.
cards: "Let us go over unto the other side of the lake." They push off, and he falls asleep in the boat. On a small boat, the mood can change in minutes.
Luke says "there came down a storm of wind on the lake." Water pours in. Some of these men are fishermen who know this lake, and they're terrified.
And the teacher is still asleep. Two stories follow, one on the water and one among graves, with a single thread: chaos, then a sudden quiet.

teach.b: They wake him: "Master, master, we perish." And Luke says: "he arose, and rebuked the wind and the raging of the water: and they ceased, and there was a calm."
The Greek for calm is galene, the glassy stillness of the sea after the wind drops. Then a question, not a lecture: "Where is your faith?"
Now they're afraid in a new way, and full of wonder: "What manner of man is this! for he commandeth even the winds and water, and they obey him."
On the far shore, in the country of the Gadarenes, pigs are feeding on the hillside. A man runs out who, Luke says, "ware no clothes, neither abode in any house, but in the tombs."
Chained and guarded, he broke free again and again.
Jesus asks a plain human question: "What is thy name?" He answers: "Legion." A legion was a Roman army unit, and Luke explains: "many devils were entered into him."
He doesn't have a name of his own anymore, just a crowd. Jesus frees him; the spirits go into the pigs, which rush into the lake.

teach.h: CLOTHED, AND IN HIS RIGHT MIND.
teach.b: The townspeople find the man "sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed, and in his right mind." The same quiet as on the lake. He begs to go with Jesus.
Jesus says no: "Return to thine own house, and shew how great things God hath done unto thee." And he goes, telling the whole city.

how: Some Christians pray with the stilling of the storm in times of fear, and the healed man sent home to tell his story is sometimes read as a picture of faith shared first with family and neighbors.

games.q: you've just been freed after years living among the tombs. you beg to go with Jesus. what does he tell you?
o: return to your own house, and tell what God has done.
go to Jerusalem and show yourself to the priests.
games.why: he sends the man home, and the man tells the whole city how much Jesus had done for him.

practice: Breathe slowly until the water inside you is a little glassier, then think of someone in a storm right now: a friend who's panicking, a child who can't sleep.

You can't command the wind, but picture yourself as the calm one in the boat, a steady voice, a slow question: what's really going on? If you pray, you can hold them before God; if you don't, simply send them stillness.

wordCard.voice: Galene, the Greek word for a calm, the glassy stillness of the sea when the wind drops: Jesus stills a storm, then frees a man among the tombs and sends him home.

carryVoice: Your line: return to your house. A week of a centurion, a widow, John's question, a woman's tears, the women who paid, good soil and a calm sea. Day five hundred thirty-two, and another week on the path.
